description: Cervical Radiculopathy Involving the C1 Nerve Root (Very Rare)

questions.prompt: Which sensory finding is present?

options.label: Residual radicular symptoms without objective sensory loss
options.help: confirms residual radicular symptoms of pain or subjectively altered sensory perception (paresthesia-like often described as numbness) without objectively verifiable sensory loss for dullness to pinprick or loss of sharp vs dull perception in a neuroanatomically plausible dermatomal distribution compatible with the C1 dermatome (ie, occipital or upper neck region, radiating from the back of the head toward the crown or forehead, with no significant limb symptoms)

questions.prompt: Is this nerve-root diagnosis supported by at least one of the listed alternatives?
questions.help:
(one of the following)
- MRI or CT imaging demonstrating a C1 nerve root injury or lesion
- electrodiagnostic findings confirming C1 nerve root pathology consistent with Guides CS definitions per Section 17.06e1 Electrodiagnosis of Radiculopathy. Although this test can assist in supporting the diagnosis, it is rarely performed and often fails to provide definitive confirmation. The primary reason lies in the technical challenges involved, as the nerve root primarily innervates muscles in the neck region and, unlike lower cervical nerve roots, lacks representation in limb muscles
- surgeon's clear objective verification of an intraoperative lesion involving the C1 nerve root

Electrodiagnostic requirements and limitations:
Electromyographic evidence is useful in detecting radicular findings, even independent of imaging studies; however, these findings must correlate with physical examination findings in order to be considered clinically significant. The presence or intensity of pain is never evaluated by electrodiagnostic studies.
For EMG findings to meet SIE criteria that qualify for radiculopathy, they must demonstrate the presence of any of following criteria at a documented skin temperature greater than 32°C in 2 or more muscles in the same limb that share the same myotome nerve root innervation:
1. Spontaneous activity (seen in acute or still active radiculopathy)
   1. Presence of multiple positive waves at rest
   2. Presence of multiple fibrillations at rest
2. Plurality of polyphasic wave forms (>30%) during muscle activation (seen in chronic radiculopathy)
3. Large-amplitude wave forms (>5 mV) during muscle activation (seen in chronic radiculopathy)
4. Increased duration (per American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine criteria) (seen in chronic radiculopathy)
5. Complex repetitive discharges recorded (chronic and rarely seen)
Electrodiagnostic testing does not detect all compressive radiculopathies, poorly detects pure sensory root involvement, and cannot determine the cause of the nerve root pathology. However, EMG can detect noncompressive radiculopathies that are not identified by imaging studies when there is axonal loss. Needle EMG findings of the paraspinal muscles in individuals with previous spine surgery or prior spine injuries must be interpreted with caution, as the paraspinal muscles may exhibit abnormalities for a prolonged time after surgery. At present, only the needle EMG is considered diagnostic for radiculopathy. H reflex, F wave, nerve conduction studies, and evoked potentials are adjuncts in the testing and can help evaluate for other pathology. Surface EMG is not currently considered diagnostic for radiculopathy or other neurological pathology.

questions.prompt: Is this nerve-root diagnosis supported by at least one of the listed alternatives?
questions.help:
(one of the following)
- MRI or CT imaging demonstrating a S1 nerve root injury or lesion
- electrodiagnostic findings confirming S1 nerve root pathology consistent with Guides CS definitions per Section 17.06e1 Electrodiagnosis of Radiculopathy. If testing meets criteria for a S1 radiculopathy by AANEM criteria. this is objective confirmation of radiculopathy. If the date of injury and date of testing align, this should be rated as radiculopathy
- surgeon's clear objective verification of an intraoperative lesion affecting the S1 nerve root

Electrodiagnostic requirements and limitations:
Electromyographic evidence is useful in detecting radicular findings, even independent of imaging studies; however, these findings must correlate with physical examination findings in order to be considered clinically significant. The presence or intensity of pain is never evaluated by electrodiagnostic studies.
For EMG findings to meet SIE criteria that qualify for radiculopathy, they must demonstrate the presence of any of following criteria at a documented skin temperature greater than 32°C in 2 or more muscles in the same limb that share the same myotome nerve root innervation:
1. Spontaneous activity (seen in acute or still active radiculopathy)
   1. Presence of multiple positive waves at rest
   2. Presence of multiple fibrillations at rest
2. Plurality of polyphasic wave forms (>30%) during muscle activation (seen in chronic radiculopathy)
3. Large-amplitude wave forms (>5 mV) during muscle activation (seen in chronic radiculopathy)
4. Increased duration (per American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine criteria) (seen in chronic radiculopathy)
5. Complex repetitive discharges recorded (chronic and rarely seen)
Electrodiagnostic testing does not detect all compressive radiculopathies, poorly detects pure sensory root involvement, and cannot determine the cause of the nerve root pathology. However, EMG can detect noncompressive radiculopathies that are not identified by imaging studies when there is axonal loss. Needle EMG findings of the paraspinal muscles in individuals with previous spine surgery or prior spine injuries must be interpreted with caution, as the paraspinal muscles may exhibit abnormalities for a prolonged time after surgery. At present, only the needle EMG is considered diagnostic for radiculopathy. H reflex, F wave, nerve conduction studies, and evoked potentials are adjuncts in the testing and can help evaluate for other pathology. Surface EMG is not currently considered diagnostic for radiculopathy or other neurological pathology.
